Suspension means the act of hanging, holding up, or temporarily stopping something — either physically in space, or in time (pausing an activity or privilege).

Think of it this way: when something is "suspended," it isn't moving forward, it isn't resting on the ground, and it isn't finished. It is held — either literally dangling, or figuratively frozen mid-action.

The word covers several distinct real-world situations. Each one is a different flavour of that same core idea.
Meaning 1: Temporarily stopping or pausing something

This is the most common, everyday meaning.

Suspension = the temporary stopping of something that was ongoing, with the understanding that it may resume.

The government announced the suspension of peace talks.
The match was delayed due to the suspension of play because of rain.
The company issued a suspension of all hiring until further notice.

The key detail is temporary. A suspension is not a cancellation, an abolition, or a permanent end. It is a pause — a "hold" button pressed on something. The implication is always that the thing could restart.

This is why you hear "suspension of services," "suspension of a law," "suspension of payments," and so on.
Meaning 2: Removing someone from their role or privilege for a period of time

This is a specific, very common use — especially in schools, workplaces, and sports.

Suspension = an official punishment or precautionary measure where a person is barred from their position, school, or activity for a fixed time.

The student received a three-day suspension for fighting.
The footballer was handed a four-match suspension for his tackle.
The employee was placed on suspension while the investigation was underway.

Here, the person still holds their position in principle — they haven't been expelled or fired permanently — but they are forbidden from exercising their role for a defined period. A suspended student is still enrolled. A suspended employee is still technically employed. That is what makes it a suspension rather than a termination.

It can also serve as a precaution (not just a punishment). Someone might be suspended while an investigation is ongoing, before any guilt is established.
Meaning 3: The physical state of hanging or being held up without full support

This is the more literal, physical meaning.

Suspension = the state in which something hangs or is supported from above, or floats within a medium, without resting on the ground.

The chandelier hung in suspension from the ceiling.
The bridge deck is kept in suspension by thick steel cables.

A suspension bridge is the perfect example here — it's a bridge where the road deck is hung (suspended) from large cables that arc overhead, anchored at both ends. The deck doesn't sit on pillars beneath it; instead, it hangs from above. That physical relationship is literally suspension.
Meaning 4: In science — a mixture of particles in a liquid (or gas)

In chemistry and science, suspension has a precise technical meaning.

A suspension = a mixture in which small, undissolved solid particles are scattered throughout a liquid (or gas), but are not dissolved into it.

Muddy water is a suspension of soil particles in water.
Calamine lotion is a suspension — that's why the bottle says "shake well before use."

This is different from a solution (like salt water), where the substance fully dissolves and you can't see the individual particles. In a suspension, the particles remain separate and visible — and given enough time, they tend to settle at the bottom. That's why many medicines and paints are suspensions that need shaking: the particles sink when left still.
Meaning 5: In vehicles — the suspension system

Vehicle suspension = the mechanical system of springs, shock absorbers, and linkages connecting a vehicle's wheels to its body, designed to absorb shocks and keep the ride smooth.

The car's suspension was damaged after hitting the pothole.
Good suspension makes a huge difference on rough roads.

Think about driving over a bump. Without suspension, every jolt from the road would be transferred directly to the passengers. The suspension system absorbs those forces — it cushions the ride. The wheels bounce and move, but the cabin stays relatively stable. The word "suspension" fits because the vehicle's body is effectively suspended — held up and isolated — from the roughness of the wheels and the road.
Meaning 6: In music — a suspended note

In music theory, a suspension is a specific technique.

Musical suspension = when a note from one chord is held over (sustained) into the next chord, where it creates a temporary tension, before resolving to the expected note.

The composer used a suspension to build tension just before the final resolution.

Imagine a chord changes, but one note stubbornly lingers from the old chord for a beat — it clashes slightly with the new chord, creating a feeling of unresolved tension. That hanging, unresolved note is the suspension. It then "resolves" by moving to the note it was always meant to land on, and the tension releases. It's one of the most powerful tools in creating emotional pull in music.

This is a phrase you'll encounter often in discussions of literature, film, and storytelling.

Suspension of disbelief = the willingness of an audience to temporarily accept things in a story that they know are not real or logically impossible, in order to enjoy the fictional experience.

Watching a superhero movie requires a suspension of disbelief.
The novel was so well-written that readers maintained their suspension of disbelief throughout.

When you watch a film where a person flies, you know that's impossible. But you choose, temporarily, to set aside your scepticism — to "suspend" your disbelief — so that you can be fully absorbed by the story. If a film is poorly made, your suspension of disbelief "breaks" and you're suddenly aware again that you're watching something fake.

The phrase was coined by the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and it has become an essential concept in how we talk about storytelling and audience engagement.
A Quick Map of All the Meanings

Suspension as pausing time → stopping an activity, service, or law temporarily.

Suspension as removing a person → barring someone from their role for a fixed period as punishment or precaution.

Suspension as hanging in space → something physically held up or dangling (suspension bridge).

Suspension as a mixture → solid particles dispersed in a liquid without dissolving (muddy water, calamine).

Suspension as a vehicle system → the mechanism that absorbs road shocks and smooths the ride.

Suspension in music → a held note that creates tension before resolving.

Suspension of disbelief → choosing to accept fiction as real, temporarily, to enjoy a story.

In every case, something is held in an in-between state:

  • A paused activity is between running and ended.
  • A suspended person is between active and dismissed.
  • A hanging object is between flying freely and resting on the ground.
  • A particle in a suspension is between dissolved and settled.
  • A vehicle's body is between the roughness of the road and a smooth cabin.
  • A suspended musical note is between one chord and its resolution.
  • A suspended belief is between full acceptance and full scepticism.

That in-between, held, neither-here-nor-there quality is the soul of the word "suspension."
